sources.news_title: Former SF GOP Chair Harmeet Dhillon Resigns From DOJ After Turbulent Tenure
sources.text:
Harmeet Dhillon resigned Thursday from the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, which she spent nearly two years reshaping around the Trump administration’s agenda, prompting a mass exodus of career attorneys and criticism from civil rights advocates.
Dhillon told Fox News that she had decided to leave three weeks earlier, before Tuesday's midterm elections, but agreed to delay announcing her departure at the request of White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, as the New York Times reports. She said she wanted to return to private practice after accomplishing what she came to Washington to do.
President Donald Trump and other White House officials were reportedly unhappy with Dhillon's recent appearance on 60 Minutes, where she downplayed the prevalence of undocumented immigrants voting, despite the administration's aggressive efforts to investigate alleged noncitizen voting.
Dhillon's tenure was defined by a sharp departure from the Civil Rights Division's traditional mission of combating racial discrimination and protecting voting rights. Under her leadership, the office increasingly focused on the Trump administration's conservative priorities, including challenging diversity, equity, and inclusion programs, investigating universities over alleged antisemitism, and pursuing restrictions on transgender rights.
Her approach, outlined in a series of April 2025 policy memos, prompted hundreds of career employees to leave. According to the Chronicle, Justice Connection, an advocacy organization made up of former Justice Department employees from both parties, reported that departures had reached approximately 75% of the division's workforce by January. The depleted staff left the office struggling to carry out its agenda, including an effort to deploy 1,000 election monitors nationwide.
Former Assistant Attorney General Kristen Clarke, who led the division during the Biden administration and is now general counsel of the NAACP, sharply criticized Dhillon's record.
“From Day 1, Harmeet Dhillon abdicated her responsibility to enforce our nation’s federal civil rights laws and destroyed the crown jewel of the Justice Department,” Clarke said, speaking to the Times.
Among Dhillon's targets were universities accused of discrimination in admissions and campus policies, as part of the Trump administration’s effort to pursue antisemitism-related cases against California's UC campuses, which largely failed to gain traction. She reportedly visited UC Berkeley last November alongside Justice Department and FBI officials after arrests outside a Turning Point USA event at Zellerbach Hall, promising a federal investigation into the school's security response.
The Chronicle reports that her office recently threatened legal action against UC Berkeley School of Law and UCSF's medical school over alleged discrimination against white and Asian students, while ending longstanding school desegregation agreements with more than 50 jurisdictions.
Further criticism followed her division's decision not to investigate the fatal ICE shooting of Renée Good earlier this year and revelations about a plan to share sensitive voter information with the Department of Homeland Security.
In her resignation letter to Trump, Dhillon cited what she considered major accomplishments, including lawsuits against DEI programs, challenges to transgender participation in women's sports, prosecutions of anti-Jewish hate crimes, and the creation of the division's first Second Amendment section.
Dhillon was also a longtime figure in San Francisco Republican politics, previously serving as chair of the San Francisco Republican Party before becoming California's Republican National Committeewoman. Per the Chronicle, she founded Dhillon Law Group and the Center for American Liberty and was part the legal team for Trump's campaign.
As SFist reported in 2023, Dhillon unsuccessfully challenged Ronna McDaniel to become chair of the Republican National Committee. That same year, Dhillon was accused of transferring $1.3 million from a nonprofit she led to her own law firm.
Other notable clients includes former Google engineer James Damore, who was fired after circulating an internal memo criticizing the company's diversity initiatives. Dhillon also pursued a short-lived lawsuit challenging San Francisco's 2020 safe sleeping site at the former Haight Street McDonald's.
Her earlier civil liberties work included defending the Sikh community against discrimination following the September 11 attacks. She also served on the ACLU of Northern California's board from 2002 to 2005 and briefly led a domestic violence nonprofit in Santa Clara County.
The Justice Department has not announced a permanent successor.

sources.text:
Harmeet Dhillon resigns as US Civil Rights chief, calls role honour of a lifetime
Harmeet Kaur Dhillon resigned as US assistant attorney general after delaying the announcement until Election Day passed. Her exit marks the Trump administration's first senior departure since the mid-term elections.
Indian-American Harmeet Kaur Dhillon has resigned as US Assistant Attorney General and head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, becoming the first senior official to leave the Trump administration since the mid-term elections, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
Dhillon said she resigned voluntarily but delayed announcing her decision at the request of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles until after Election Day.
Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the resignation on social media, saying Dhillon had “led the Civil Rights Division with conviction”. “She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favour,” Blanche wrote on X on Thursday. “The department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavours,” he added.
Dhillon, whose law firm was part of Donald Trump's campaign legal team, told Fox News that she had resigned of her own volition, according to PTI.
“Serving my country as AAG for Civil Rights has been the honour of a lifetime. We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls' sports, and so much more. I want to thank President Trump for giving me this opportunity. I look forward to what's next,” she said in a post on X.
Born in Chandigarh into a Punjabi Sikh family, Dhillon moved with her parents first to London and later to the United States. A staunch ally of President Donald Trump, she ran her own law firm in San Francisco for several years before joining the Justice Department.
Dhillon is a frequent guest on conservative podcasts and is highly active on social media. Unlike her predecessors, she regularly posted videos about the work of her division. In media interviews, she acknowledged that social media posts often gave her ideas for civil rights investigations.
At a Moms for Liberty event in New York in May, Dhillon described moving to the US as the “greatest gift” her parents had given her. “My dad was an orthopaedic surgeon. Mom and Dad left India in the 1970s because it was a Russian client state. They had a dictated two-children policy and a planned economy, and Mom and Dad didn't want to raise their kids in that kind of an environment, so they came to America,” said Dhillon, who rose to prominence as a civil rights attorney.
“Besides life, the greatest gift that Mom and Dad gave me was bringing me here to America and allowing me to be sworn in as a naturalised American citizen when I was 10 years old,” she said. Dhillon said her parents moved to the US when the country faced a shortage of doctors and Washington was inviting medical professionals during the Vietnam War.
Dhillon's departure ends her tenure as head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division after she delayed the announcement until the elections were over.

sources.news_title: The DOJ official who spent 19 months terrorizing colleges is resigning
sources.text:
Misery loves company, and for the past 19 months, American colleges have had plenty of both, largely thanks to Harmeet K. Dhillon, the Justice Department’s assistant attorney general for civil rights, who has spent her entire tenure treating campuses like crime scenes.
Dhillon undid years of diversity, equity, and inclusion work at more than 300 colleges by launching aggressive investigations, lawsuits, and pressure campaigns. Now she’s leaving because she didn’t get a promotion.
Dhillon had become increasingly frustrated that she had not been promoted to a higher post, MS NOW reported. She told the administration before the midterms that she planned to step down after the election.
“Serving my country as AAG for Civil Rights has been the honor of a lifetime,” Dhillon wrote Thursday on X. “We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls’ sports, and so much more.”
She’s being modest. Under Dhillon, the Justice Department stopped investigating accusations of systemic racism or sexism and declined to investigate ICE officers’ fatal shootings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis earlier this year. Tasked with protecting the rights of people with disabilities, Dhillon has also used the r-word in casual social media posts.
Dhillon also turned the Civil Rights division of the Justice Department—created to repair the injustices of Jim Crow—into a relentless legal sledgehammer aimed at universities with programs that uplifted marginalized groups.
Since starting the job in April 2025, Dhillon has bragged about opening more than 100 investigations into university admissions practices, accusing colleges of discrimination for maintaining race-conscious programs and of antisemitism for allowing pro-Palestinian activism on campus.
In a way, she was wildly successful. Since 2024, more than 300 campuses have eliminated DEI requirements, closed DEI offices, removed diversity statements from hiring processes, and changed or removed their DEI policies.
“She has corrupted [the Civil Rights Division’s] mission,” Vanita Gupta, a former head of the DOJ civil rights division under President Joe Biden, told the New York Times in August.
The repercussions of Dhillon’s efforts “will be felt for decades and decades,” Nina Beattie, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, told the Boston Globe in March. “All of the advances that we’ve made in civil rights and equality over the years, they’ve just now been pushed back decades.”
At her alma mater, the University of Virginia, Dhillon opened a slew of investigations that prompted the university president—a law school classmate of hers who led efforts to diversify the student body—to resign. Perhaps her most high-profile foe has been Harvard University, which has repeatedly challenged the DOJ’s lawsuits as other universities capitulated. This spring, Dhillon sued Harvard twice in the span of six weeks, accusing the university of tolerating antisemitism and withholding race-related admissions data from the government.
Federal judges dismissed both suits.
Dhillon is the first senior official out the door since Democrats trounced the GOP in races up and down the ballot this week. She may not be the last. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is reportedly weighing whether to call it quits, too.

sources.text:
Head of Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division resigns
(CBS NEWS) — Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, resigned on Thursday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said.
“Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division with conviction the past 18 months,” Blanche wrote in a post on X. “She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor. The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors.”
Dhillon oversaw a mass exodus from the Civil Rights Division last year, with more than 75% of its staff departing. She overhauled a division that had long prioritized fighting discrimination against some of the nation’s most vulnerable and historically marginalized groups.
Since taking over the division, often lauded as being the “crown jewel” of the DOJ, she has reoriented it to focus instead on other priorities that have included protecting gun owners’ rights, curbing the use of equity, diversity and inclusion policies at universities, and adopting legal positions that oppose civil rights protections for transgender people.
In her resignation letter to President Trump, which was seen by CBS News, Dhillon said that she told White House chief of staff Susie Wiles in early October that she intended to step down after the midterm elections.
Two sources familiar with the matter, however, told CBS News that Trump demanded she be fired after he watched her Oct. 18 appearance on “60 Minutes” discussing the government’s election integrity efforts.
In that interview, Dhillon touted the Justice Department’s efforts to prosecute noncitizens who unlawfully voted in prior elections, noting that the Biden administration had only prosecuted 13 people while the Trump investigation was investigating “thousands” of such cases.
In her resignation letter, Dhillon touted her efforts to end “unlawful and discriminatory DEI practices” and to protect “women and girls’ sports from biological males, including through lawsuits against Minnesota and California,” among other accomplishments.
“While I am leaving this post, I will continue fighting for our country in the years ahead,” she added.
During her tenure, the Justice Department closed many of its cases involving discrimination targeting Black Americans and announced it had dismissed more than 50 decades-old consent decrees with public schools, many in the Deep South, that were in place to protect Black students from unlawful discrimination.
Dhillon nixed two pending consent decrees last year with the Minneapolis and Louisville Police Departments over systemic abuses that were investigated in the wake of the killings of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor and rescinded the investigative findings of misconduct into six other police departments.
Earlier this year, after immigration agents shot and killed American citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis as they were protesting the administration’s immigration crackdown, the Civil Rights Division did not move to open any criminal civil rights investigations, in violation of longstanding practice for such high-profile officer-involved shootings.
The division ultimately got involved in the Pretti case after the Justice Department faced staunch criticism and questions about why Homeland Security Investigations — and not the FBI — was leading the probe into its own agency.
To date, no charges have been filed in the Pretti case, which is also separately under investigation by state officials.

sources.news_title: Harmeet Dhillon, Trump ally and head of DOJ civil rights unit, resigns
sources.text:
U.S. Justice Department official Harmeet Dhillon, who reshaped the agency’s civil rights unit to pursue Trump administration priorities including voter data requests and gun rights cases, has resigned, Attorney-General Todd Blanche said on Thursday.
Dhillon is among the first senior officials to leave the administration after Tuesday’s midterm elections, in which Democrats retook both chambers of Congress.
Dhillon, a Trump ally, oversaw an overhaul of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, which has historically enforced laws protecting voting rights and fighting racial discrimination. Under her leadership, the division shifted focus toward challenging diversity initiatives and investigating antisemitism on college campuses, leading to probes of several elite universities.
The changes prompted a wave of departures among career staff. Dhillon said attorneys in the unit pursued liberal priorities and were unwilling to implement Trump’s agenda.

In a resignation letter, Dhillon cited as accomplishments efforts to force U.S. institutions to scale back diversity initiatives and challenges to school districts over transgender policies. She said she told the White House in October she planned to resign.
“We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls’ sports, and so much more,” Dhillon posted on social media, thanking Trump for the appointment.
She will return to her law firm, The Dhillon Law Group, according to her spokesperson. Her firm had recently shrunk as some attorneys left for other practices.
Two people familiar with the matter said Dhillon was frustrated that she had been passed over for promotions in the department and wanted to return to her firm to reinvigorate it.
The Civil Rights Division in prior administrations conducted investigations into police departments accused of systematic civil rights violations, including after high-profile killings of Black people by local police.
“For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded,” said Stacey Young, the head of Justice Connection, an advocacy group. “Dhillon decimated it.”
Dhillon withdrew earlier findings from those police probes and investigated whether some Democratic-led cities violated people’s gun rights under the Second Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.
Dhillon led investigations to pressure dozens of universities she viewed as too liberal. Many of those centred on alleged antisemitism, diversity initiatives, and treatment of transgender people.
Those probes helped the department extract hundreds of millions of dollars in settlement agreements from some of the nation’s premier universities, and even led to the resignation of the president of the University of Virginia. One high-profile target, Harvard University, refused to pay a large settlement and instead has repeatedly fought the Trump administration in court.
Ahead of the midterms, the division played a major role in the Trump administration’s efforts to prevent non-citizens from voting, a phenomenon that independent reviews have found is exceedingly rare. The DOJ lost a series of cases to obtain private voter data from states and deployed about 1,000 staff to monitor polling sites during Tuesday’s vote.
Dhillon has also been involved in cases against perceived Trump enemies.
The civil rights unit brought a high-profile criminal case against former CNN anchor Don Lemon and others accused of disrupting a church service in January to protest the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota.
The division also sought unsuccessfully to bring criminal charges against Cassidy Hutchinson, a former White House aide who gave vivid testimony to Congress about Trump’s actions on the day of the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot.

Dhillon drastically reshaped the Civil Rights Division, which was created in 1957 to protect “the civil and constitutional rights of all persons in the United States by enforcing anti-discrimination laws,” according to the official website.

"We don’t just slow down the woke," Dhillon said at a Federalist Society event in 2025. "We take up the cause to achieve the executive branch's goals."
Her exit was celebrated by LGBTQ+ groups.

Bloomberg (opens in new tab) was first to report the news.
Dhillon is the first senior Justice Department official to resign after Democrats’ wins in Tuesday’s midterms, which will give the party control of both the House and Senate. She told Bloomberg in August that she intended to return to her California firm, Dhillon Law Group, after her time in government.
A frequent Fox News guest, Dhillon founded the San Francisco-based Dhillon Law Group in 2006. The firm championed conservative legal battles, such as suing UC Berkeley over its free speech policies and antifa activists for allegedly assaulting conservative journalists. It also sued several states over their COVID-19 policies.
In 2023, she was appointed to head the Republican Party’s election integrity efforts, much of which relied on false claims that Trump won the 2020 election.
Over her 20-year rise in San Francisco, many local politicos saw her as a collegial Republican with whom they could work. After the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks, Dhillon served on the board of the American Civil Liberties Union, an organization generally viewed as left-leaning.
“During that period of time, I always found Harmeet to be a really pleasant person, smart and very moderate, very middle of the road, even lefty on some issues,” Democratic state Sen. Scott Wiener told The Standard in 2025.
Opponents criticized her tenure at the DOJ as partisan and aimed at fundamentally changing the nature of the Civil Rights Division.
“Since taking office, Dhillon has operated not as a law enforcement official faithfully executing civil rights statutes but, like Bondi, as a partisan operative dismantling and perverting the very infrastructure she was confirmed to lead,” the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights (opens in new tab) said.
Under her tenure, three-quarters of the division’s staff have been pushed out or left of their own accord. In a 2025 letter, more than 200 staffers said the Trump administration and Dhillon had perverted the division’s mission.
“She abruptly announced new mission statements that included fighting diversity initiatives instead of race-based discrimination, investigating baseless allegations of voter fraud rather than protecting the right to vote,” the group of employees wrote (opens in new tab).
Under her leadership, the division shifted its focus toward religious liberty and Second Amendment rights. It also pursued cases involving voter rolls, immigration, and antisemitism on college campuses. Career attorneys left in large numbers. The department then recruited dozens of lawyers with conservative advocacy backgrounds.

This week, she heralded (opens in new tab) a deployment of election monitors in all 50 states. She called election integrity “one of the top priorities for this administration and this division,” intended to achieve “transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner.”
Many state officials described the monitoring as an effort to meddle in elections (opens in new tab), PBS reported.
Born in India, Dhillon moved to the United States with her family, who settled in North Carolina. She graduated from high school at 16 and started college that same year. For nearly a decade, she played a prominent role in California’s Republican Party and, to a lesser degree, the national party.
In 2016, she gave the opening prayer at the party’s national convention. As a Republican National Committee member for the state, she gave a prayer at the party’s 2024 convention that drew far-right backlash (opens in new tab), the Guardian reported.

Patrick Davis, who led the Office of Legislative Affairs, resigned (opens in new tab) in October. In her year and a half as Assistant Attorney General, Dhillon upended the division in an attempt to reshape its work to fit into the Trump era — shifting from its traditional work enforcing laws encouraging elections access and police reform to fighting what she has called “woke ideology.”
In recent weeks, Dhillon, a former legal adviser to President Donald Trump’s campaign, appeared increasingly sidelined as the department pursued a series of high-profile election-related legal cases of high interest to the president.
“Where’s Harmeet?” asked one GOP official working on some of the legal cases the department pursued to try to support Trump’s claims of Democrats trying to steal the election.
Dhillon took on a high profile albeit non-traditional presence on social media, announcing initiatives alongside her love of knitting, while embracing right-wing causes, including opening a section dedicated to the Second Amendment and promoting gun ownership.
She leaves behind a division faltering due to a lack of staffing — more than 75% of the Civil Rights Division was fired or quit during her term. She recruited several conservative lawyers to join the division in their place, but those hires have far from made up for the ouster of decades of knowledge on civil rights laws.

Harmeet Dhillon, California attorney who radically reshaped DOJ civil rights unit, resigns
- Click here to listen to this article

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Harmeet Dhillon has resigned after leading a sweeping overhaul of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division.
- Many career civil rights attorneys left the department after she took over and demanded an ideological shift in the work.
- The division has dropped police reform cases and pursued investigations of universities and voter records. Former attorneys say it abandoned its traditional civil rights mission.
Assistant Atty. Gen. Harmeet Dhillon, a California attorney who radically reshaped the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division to focus on political issues important to President Trump — including by targeting transgender rights and launching a nationwide hunt for alleged voter fraud by noncitizens — resigned her post Thursday.
In a resignation letter and in a post to X — where she routinely lambasted liberal policy and touted her office’s legal work to dismantle it — Dhillon said serving as the division’s chief was an honor.
“We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls’ sports, and so much more,” she wrote on X. “I want to thank President Trump for giving me this opportunity. I look forward to what’s next!”
Critics of Dhillon — including prominent civil rights leaders who had opposed her confirmation to the post — cheered her departure, saying she had flipped the storied Civil Rights Division on its head by attacking pillars of its past work, such as affirmative action policies, diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives, LGBTQ+ rights and voting rights.
“Is Harmeet running from a sinking ship? Trying to avoid actual oversight? Or getting pushed out by DOJ leadership?” Vanita Gupta, who headed the Civil Rights Division under President Obama, said in a text message. “Maybe it’s all of the above but regardless, she used the Civil Rights Division against the very communities and values it was founded to protect and that will be her legacy.”
Another part of her legacy, Gupta said, will be that she “oversaw the decimation of the Division’s incredible career workforce.” Many career civil rights attorneys left the department after she took over and demanded an ideological shift in the work.
Dhillon’s departure comes two days after a midterm election in which Republicans suffered sweeping losses, and amid widespread speculation as to how Trump and other leaders in his administration would respond — and who among them, if any, would leave or be unceremoniously ousted. Turnover after such an electoral drubbing is not uncommon.
In her resignation letter, Dhillon said she initially resigned in October, but that White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles asked her to stay on until after the midterms. Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that Dhillon did “a fantastic job ... boldly protecting Americans’ civil liberties.”
California has been the target of more civil rights actions than any other state. The civil rights division is led by California-native Harmeet Dhillon.
Dhillon also touted what she called “historic victories for the American people” under her leadership, and specifically cited her work ending diversity, equity and inclusion programs, suing states including California over their policies for transgender students and athletes and for their voter rolls, defending gun rights and fighting anti-Semitism.
Dhillon’s success in those initiatives was middling at best — and in some areas disastrous. Out of dozens of lawsuits demanding states turn over their voter rolls, for instance, she had zero wins.
Atty. Gen. Todd Blanche, on X, wrote that Dhillon “has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor,” and that the department “is grateful for her dedicated public service” and wished her “every success in her future endeavors.”
A spokesperson for Dhillon said she was returning to her firm, the Dhillon Law Group.
Mark Trammell, the chief executive of the conservative Center for American Liberty — which Dhillon founded — praised her work in the Justice Department as “advancing civil rights for all Americans.”
Others expressed stridently different feelings about her tenure.
Stacey Young, executive director of Justice Connection, a nonprofit organization of former Justice Department employees that advocates for a non-politicized department, blasted Dhillon’s tenure in the department and cheered her departure.
“Harmeet Dhillon has been the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history,” Young said in a statement. “After she upended the division’s mission-critical work, the civil servants who dedicated their careers to protecting vulnerable communities were instead told to target them — and more than three-quarters of the division’s lawyers left.”
Dhillon turned away from the division’s traditional role of investigating problematic police departments and rebuffed calls for federal civil rights investigations into the killing by immigration agents of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis. She later relented amid intense public pressure to launch an investigation into Pretti’s killing, but was criticized for assigning inexperienced staff and not taking the inquiry seriously.
Dhillon also helped dismantle long-standing firewalls between the Justice Department and the White House, acknowledging that she saw her mission as pursuing civil rights in line with Trump’s executive orders.
She focused on targeting universities accused of discriminating against white and Asian students, attacking policies protecting transgender students and athletes in California and elsewhere, and launching her failed nationwide effort to obtain state voter rolls in order to root out alleged noncitizen voters.
She also took a leading role in threatening election workers processing ballots in the midterms.
As of Thursday morning, Dhillon still had pinned to the top of her X account a post from July, in which she discussed sending letters to elections officials in all 50 states warning them that it is a crime to knowingly process ballots from noncitizens.
“Every state and local election official is on notice — knowingly encouraging noncitizens to vote or conspiring to fraudulently register noncitizens is a federal crime,” she wrote.
L.A. County says it has received federal grand jury subpoenas demanding voter registration information on dozens of individuals the Trump administration suspects may not be U.S. citizens.
Before being appointed to the Justice Department, Dhillon had made a name for herself in California by attacking transgender rights and challenging COVID-19 pandemic restrictions and voting rights initiatives.
California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta, asked about Dhillon’s departure, said, “Good riddance.”
“Few people have done more to undermine U.S. DOJ’s civil rights legacy than Harmeet Dhillon — undermining free and fair elections, subverting anti-discrimination laws, and targeting marginalized communities,” Bonta said — efforts he said his office helped thwart in court.
Brian Levin, a professor emeritus of Cal State San Bernardino and founder of the Center for the Study of Hate and Extremism, said Dhillon’s tenure atop the Civil Rights Division “was nothing short of an unmitigated catastrophe” compared with the division’s work under past Republican and Democratic administrations.
Levin said Dhillon ignored data showing discrimination against “the very vulnerable communities for whom the Civil Rights Division” was created to help to instead focus on things like “anti-white discrimination” and gun rights — overseeing “a complete abdication of protecting voting rights, housing and a slew of other projects that have been the foundation of what the division was founded to do.”
Levin said that “among these vulnerable communities that need the help the most that she has turned her back on have been the gay community, the trans community, immigrants, racial minorities, as well as the disabled,” and accused Dhillon of having “butchered” the division’s career staff and replaced it with people who “were vastly underqualified.”
“She was horrible, and anyone who cares about the preservation of civil rights, ... and those who are the most vulnerable in our society, while not rejoicing today, can at least take some solace that the hemorrhaging will at least temporarily stop,” Levin said.
Young, of the Justice Connection, called on the next Senate — which will have a Democratic majority thanks to Tuesday’s elections — to exercise its confirmation powers to ensure Dhillon’s successor atop the Civil Rights Division fulfills its “congressional mandate to enforce all Americans’ civil rights diligently and fairly.”

Donald Trump’s chief of the storied Civil Rights Division at the Department of Justice has resigned, marking the first top administration official to leave the administration after Republicans suffered brutal losses in midterm elections this week.
Harmeet Dhillon — who steered the agency away from critical missions like protecting voting rights, police oversight and combating racial discrimination during her 18 months at the Justice Department — submitted her resignation Thursday.
“She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor,” Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Thursday.
“The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors,” he added.
Dhillon, an attorney who supported the president’s efforts to reverse his election loss in 2020 and joined his “election integrity” team in 2024, had refocused the Civil Rights Division to investigate what she called “woke ideology,” including transgender athletes in girls’ and women’s sports, “anti-Christian bias,” and institutions with diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives, among other culture war issues that departed from the department’s core mission to combat discrimination and protect the rights of historically marginalized groups.
In her resignation letter to the president, Dhillon said she told White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles in October that she was planning to leave the administration. “I resigned three weeks ago, and Susie asked me to please wait until after the midterms,” she told Fox News.
“Consistent with that conversation, I hereby resign as Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights at the United States Department of Justice,” she wrote Thursday. “Serving you and your Administration has been the greatest honor of my lifetime. Thank you for giving me this opportunity.”
She had reportedly grown frustrated with other top Justice Department officials as she was allegedly overlooked for other senior roles at the agency, according to MSNOW.
And according to The New York Times, the president and other White House officials were unhappy about her comments to 60 Minutes that they allegedly believe had downplayed the idea of noncitizen voting — a key target in the administration’s legal threats to state election officials in the weeks leading up to the midterms.
“While I am leaving this post, I will continue fighting for our country in the years ahead. Thank you again,” Dhillon wrote.
She will return to Dhillon Law Group, the California-based law firm she founded.
In response to requests for comment, the Justice Department sent The Independent a post from X with Blanche’s brief statement.
Still, the timing of her departure follows blowout losses for the president’s party, with incoming congressional Democrats preparing to investigate administration officials across the government.
Under her leadership at the Justice Departments “crown jewel,” the Civil Rights Division dropped lawsuits intended to protect voting rights and instead pivoted to aggressive federal intervention in election administration, with the agency’s pivotal Voting Section turning into an arm of the administration’s attempts to obtain sensitive voter data and investigate alleged voter fraud.
In the leadup to the 2026 midterms, her office filed lawsuits against 30 states and Washington, D.C., to obtain voter registration lists — and federal judges tossed out 27 of them.
“Harmeet is one of the top Election lawyers in the Country, fighting to ensure that all, and ONLY, legal votes are counted,” Trump said in a statement announcing Dhillon’s nomination in 2024. “In her new role at the DOJ, Harmeet will be a tireless defender of our Constitutional Rights, and will enforce our Civil Rights and Election Laws FAIRLY and FIRMLY.”
She mounted the largest-ever deployment of election monitors in Justice Department history, sending more than 900 election observers to polling locations in all 50 states, a move that voting rights advocates condemned as unconstitutional voter intimidation.

Earlier this year, Dhillon’s office also announced that the Justice Department was abandoning investigations into allegations of police misconduct, constitutional violations and civil rights abuses in the wake of high-profile police killings.
She experienced a mass exodus of hundreds of career officials and government attorneys who resigned or were forced out under her watch. More than 75 percent of the division’s staff left the agency within the last two years.
“Harmeet Dhillon has been the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history,” according to Stacey Young, executive director of Justice Connection, a group of former Justice Department officials speaking out against the administration’s upheaval of the agency.
“Americans’ civil rights don’t enforce themselves. For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded. Dhillon decimated it,” Young said.

Harmeet Dhillon, who ran the Justice Department’s Civil Rights division, resigns
By Hannah Rabinowitz, Evan Perez, CNN
(CNN) — Harmeet Dhillon has resigned from her post as the head of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, making her the first senior official to leave the administration since the midterms.
Attorney General Todd Blanche announced her resignation in a social media post, saying that she has “led the Civil Rights Division with conviction.”
“She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor,” Blanche wrote on X “The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors.”
In her year and a half as Assistant Attorney General, Dhillon upended the division in an attempt to reshape its work to fit into the Trump era — shifting from its traditional work enforcing laws encouraging elections access and police reform to fighting what she has called “woke ideology.”
In recent weeks, Dhillon, a former legal adviser to President Donald Trump’s campaign, appeared increasingly sidelined as the department pursued a series of high-profile election-related legal cases of high interest to the president.
“Where’s Harmeet?” asked one GOP official working on some of the legal cases the department pursued to try to support Trump’s claims of Democrats trying to steal the election.
Dhillon took on a high profile albeit non-traditional presence on social media, announcing initiatives alongside her love of knitting, while embracing right-wing causes, including opening a section dedicated to the Second Amendment and promoting gun ownership.
She leaves behind a division faltering due to a lack of staffing — more than 75% of the Civil Rights Division was fired or quit during her term. She recruited several conservative lawyers to join the division in their place, but those hires have far from made up for the ouster of decades of knowledge on civil rights laws.
In fact, the gutting of the Civil Rights Division was part of the problem for Dhillon because some conservatives complained that inexperienced lawyers in her section weren’t able to handle cases referred to her division.
Dhillon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Dhillon’s departure was all but guaranteed to come in the days following the election. Her control over the Civil Rights Division had been declining for months, officials familiar with the matter said, in part because of her repeated losses in court and the perception among colleagues that she was good at announcing initiatives and less effective at accomplishing them.
The largest losses Dhillon suffered in court were over her attempts to gain access to voter rolls. Judges across the country tossed lawsuits that Dhillon claimed would help states “clean” their rolls of non-citizens, sharply criticizing what they saw as an effort to use the law to disenfranchise voters or access their personal data.
Dhillon was increasingly sidelined from the department’s voting efforts as the midterms approached, sources told CNN. As the election approached, it was Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter who signed on to the highest profile lawsuits, not Dhillon.
Stanley Woodward, Associate Attorney General, with whom Dhillon had a strained relationship, took the lead appearing in court defending the administration’s legal moves.
Still, other efforts she spearheaded came with mixed success. She sent letters to and filed lawsuits against universities she accused of brad antisemitism and discrimination largely against white students, for example, gut those efforts rarely resulted in a court win — or even in a lawsuit at all.
Some of the universities committed to help root out antisemitism, but sources have told CNN there was little framework or follow up from the department at all.

Top Justice Department Official Resigns as Rats Begin Jumping
Harmeet Dhillon, who led some of Trump’s worst crusades at the Justice Department, quit after the Republicans wiped out this election.
Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty Images
Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon is leaving the Trump administration.
Fox News reports that Dhillon resigned Thursday following Democrats’ landslide victory in the midterm elections. She reportedly told allies that she planned to leave after the elections, according to Bloomberg Law.
Dhillon is the first top official to leave the Trump administration following the election. She overhauled her division at the DOJ to actually weaken civil rights, and on diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives, said, “Either DEI will end on its own or we will kill it.” She also staffed the civil rights office with the worst lawyers, including people with criminal records, misconduct allegations, a love of conspiracy theories, and a history of hacking election sites. Dhillon also led a sweeping campaign to force states to turn over sensitive voter information, a crusade repeatedly shut down in court.
In September, Dhillon proudly announced that the DOJ had dropped more than 50 desegregation cases, most of which were in Southern states with Jim Crow histories. On her watch, the office focuses on everything but civil rights, looking at election rolls, immigration, and alleged antisemitism on college campuses.
Dhillon’s departure could be the first sign of people fleeing a highly unpopular, lame-duck administration. Others could be fired, such as Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, whom Trump has been considering giving the axe. White House adviser and deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller has plenty of enemies upset that his hard-line immigration policies made Republicans massively unpopular.
Trump Is Losing Power. Marco Rubio’s Next Move Proves It.
The secretary of state is preparing to make a massive break with Donald Trump.
Peter Zay/Anadolu/Getty Images
The MAGA movement’s Tuesday bloodbath has already inspired some of the far-right contingent’s biggest figureheads to plot a course without Donald Trump.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio is preparing to resign from the Trump administration as he lays the groundwork for a potential 2028 presidential campaign, The Independent reported Thursday.
Insiders in Washington and the British government told the newspaper that Rubio needs to distance himself from Trump’s controversies—including the wildly unpopular war in Iran—to improve his odds at the ballot box.
The news would be a major snub to Vice President JD Vance, who has been teasing his own presidential bid for months and has long been viewed as Trump’s only clear successor.
Both the White House and the State Department refuted reports of Rubio’s forthcoming exit, telling the Independent that the allegations were “baseless.” But the possible Republican challenge may not have come as a surprise to Trump himself, who speculated to reporters Wednesday that “maybe [Vance] won’t run.”
“We’ll see what happens. Everybody—You don’t know who’s talking about running. You could have a lot of people, maybe a lot of people running, maybe nobody is gonna run. Maybe he won’t run. I don’t know who’s going to run,” Trump said, before adding that he “wouldn’t have done nothing different” regarding the Iran war.
If Rubio does decide to leave, he will leave behind a shattered and broken White House that is on the cusp of losing even more Cabinet members as Trump looks for places to lay blame for his shoddy second term.
Last month, Trump reportedly called several close confidantes to assess the potential of using White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, his former campaign manager and famed “Ice Maiden,” as a scapegoat for a major midterm bust. He’s also made the rounds to check current attitudes about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman General Dan Caine as the Iran war drags on into its eighth month.
But even more heads could roll after January, when Democrats retake both chambers of Congress. Liberal party leaders indicated Thursday that they plan to make Washington a very different place in the new year. Some Republicans seem to be in agreement: Representative Thomas Massie plans to resurrect his articles of impeachment against Hegseth, and several members of the GOP believe it will pass.
Pete Hegseth May Get Impeached Before Dems Even Take Over Congress
Republican Representative Thomas Massie plans to file articles of impeachment when Congress resumes session.
Aaron Favila/AFP/Getty Images
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth doesn’t need a blue wave to knock him out of office—Republicans are already pissed enough on their own.
Outgoing Representative Thomas Massie told CNN Wednesday that he plans to trigger a vote to impeach Hegseth when Congress returns next week. Multiple GOP sources said they expect the measure to pass.
Massie introduced his impeachment articles in mid-September as a privileged resolution, requiring the House to vote on it within two days. House Speaker Mike Johnson called an early campaign-season recess in order to kill the measure, but Massie told a reporter that he’d take up the effort after the midterm elections.
Following previous reporting that Donald Trump intended to oust Hegseth as the fall guy for the Republicans disastrous midterm elections, the president told ABC News Thursday that he had “every intention to keep him.”
Massie had his own response. “If Trump’s going to replace appointees like Hegseth, he should do it while he can still get the replacements confirmed in the Senate,” he wrote on X Thursday. “Also, my Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dem’s control Congress. They’ll have hearings & trials.”
The previous evening, Massie had warned, “There is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns.”
While House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has suggested that Democrats are not interested in “getting even” with Republicans, he indicated Thursday that the Defense secretary would be a potential target when he became House Speaker.
“Why is Pete Hegseth still around?” Jeffries wrote on X.
Trump Begs to Win a Single Midterm Election in Panicked Rant
Donald Trump is losing it over his party’s midterm performance.
Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
Donald Trump is trying to rig another election.
The president suggested making an eyebrow-raising change to the Alaska Senate race, writing on Truth Social on Thursday that the votes cast for independent candidate Dan J. Sullivan Jr. should be tacked on to the vote count for incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan.
“The vote totals for the Fake Dan Sullivan, plus the other ‘slug’ that the Dems put on the Ballot, should be immediately given to the REAL Dan Sullivan, and the Election is over—He easily wins,” Trump wrote. “There is no other fair solution!”
Sullivan is currently neck and neck in the Alaska race with his Democratic opponent, Mary Peltola. As of the time of publication, Peltola has 48.17 percent of the vote, while Sullivan has 47.88 percent. Sullivan Jr., meanwhile, has 1.68 percent of the vote. Combining the results for the two Sullivans would squeeze the Republican ahead of Peltola, though actually doing so would violate the law.
Alaska is still tabulating its votes, however: Just 74 percent of the Last Frontier has reported its Election Day results. The state also uses ranked-choice voting, meaning it could take longer to count the rankings, as well.
Whether Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher, decided to enter the midterms by his own accord is currently in doubt. The New York Times reported last week that he was recruited by individuals connected to Peltola’s campaign. On Saturday, CBS News reported that the political independent had left his hometown and flown to Anchorage. In his own words, Sullivan wrote on Facebook in June that he entered this race because he was “unhappy with the 12 year record of the current Senator” and felt that “we need a change.”
“It’s that simple,” he said.
Republicans didn’t buy it. Party leaders have since accused Democrats of election fraud and of attempting to brew confusion about the ballot ahead of Election Day. Alaskans, in turn, have argued that they’re not confused by the situation at all. One Anchorage resident told CNN last week that the controversy had not shaken his vote, informing the network that you can “absolutely” tell who’s who on the ballot.
“And I don’t even have my glasses on,” he quipped. “It’s pretty clear. It’s in black and white.”
But the Trump administration is still trying to change the record. In other panicked missives, Trump has called for criminal prosecution of Peltola, and directed the Justice Department to sue Alaska and its election officials in a flagrant attempt to block the certification of the vote if the Republican Sullivan loses. The DOJ has already issued letters to a number of prominent Democrats informing them that they may be targets of a federal investigation.
James Talarico Won Texas Before Election Day Even Started
Texas’s Senate election was over before it began.
James Talarico on Election Night
Brandon Bell/Getty Images
James Talarico on Election Night
Democrat James Talarico didn’t just win big in Texas’s Senate race—he won before Election Day.
According to data from the Texas secretary of state’s office, Talarico got 4,397,474 votes in early voting—more than the 4,249,373 votes that his Republican opponent, Texas Attorney General James Paxton, received overall. While the election results have not been certified by the state of Texas yet, all 5,303 polling locations and 254 counties in the state were reporting results, according to the secretary of state’s website.
Texas Secretary of State
The total margin of victory stands at 55 percent for Talarico versus 43 percent for Paxton, greater than the 50–43 margin the last poll predicted before the election. Texas has a 12-day early voting period, and it shattered its own turnout records, with 7.4 million Texans voting during that time.
Talarico’s win was already historic, as he is the first Democrat elected to represent Texas in the Senate since 1988, when then-incumbent Lloyd Bentsen won reelection. But a win by 12 percentage points, in a state Trump won by 13.7 percentage points in 2024, shows just how unpopular Republicans were in these midterms.
And Talarico was not the only Democrat to win in Texas: The party swept every statewide race, is on track to take over the state House, and flipped all four of the state Supreme Court seats that were on the ballot. Texans not only followed the rest of the country in punishing Republicans during these midterms, but they came out in large numbers early, and upended decades of GOP dominance.

Dhillon had been a powerful and divisive figure inside President Donald Trump’s Justice Department since her confirmation last year as assistant attorney general, where she dramatically changed the direction of a division created during the country’s Civil Rights Movement to protect the rights of minorities.
“We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls’ sports, and so much more,” Dhillon said in a social media post announcing her departure, using the acronym for diversity, equity and inclusion. She called serving in the position “the honor of a lifetime.”

More than three quarters of the unit’s workforce at the beginning of Trump’s second term have left — a move Dhillon has called the “biggest single personnel self-purge in DOJ history.”
She accused the past administration of pursuing a misguided liberal agenda and welcomed the departures of attorneys not aligned with the Trump administration’s priorities, saying in an interview last year with conservative pundit Glenn Beck that “the job here is to enforce the federal civil rights laws — not woke ideology.”
Attorney General Todd Blanche wrote in a social media post announcing Dhillon’s departure that she had led the division with “conviction” and “defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor.”
“The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors,” Blanche wrote.

“Americans’ civil rights don’t enforce themselves. For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded,” Young said in an emailed statement Thursday. “Dhillon decimated it.”
Dhillon, who was born in India and immigrated with her Sikh family to the United States as a child, was a prominent figure in conservative legal and political circles well before being tapped to her Justice Department position.

‘I Wasn’t Asked to Resign’: Harmeet Dhillon Resigns as Head of Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division
- According to some reports, her exit had long been expected after President Trump privately voiced frustration with the division's mounting, embarrassing court losses.
Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general who led the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division for about 18 months, resigned Thursday, Nov. 5. Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the resignation in a post on X, praising her for leading the division “with conviction.”
She is the first senior official to leave the Trump administration since Tuesday’s midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of the House and Senate, according to The Washington Post. Her tenure remade one of the department’s best-known divisions. Supporters describe it as an overdue correction; critics describe it as dismantling the division.
Why She Left: Two Accounts
Her version. Dhillon told Fox News Digital that the decision was hers and came weeks before the election. “I wasn’t asked to resign,” she said. She said she told White House chief of staff Susie Wiles about three weeks before Election Day that she had accomplished what she came to do and wanted to return to private practice, and that Wiles asked her to wait until after the midterms. Forbes, citing The Washington Post, reported that her resignation letter says she informed Wiles in October. She has said she plans to return to her firm, Dhillon Law Group, according to Bloomberg, as cited by The Daily Signal.
The reported backdrop. Other outlets, citing unnamed sources, describe a weakening position. ABC News reported that her exit had long been expected after President Trump privately voiced frustration with the division’s mounting, embarrassing court losses. CNN reported that her control over the division had been slipping for months. Officials told CNN this was partly because of those losses, and partly because colleagues saw her as better at announcing initiatives than carrying them out. CNN also reported that some conservatives complained the division’s newer, less experienced lawyers could not handle cases referred to it. Dhillon did not address those reports in her Fox interview.
A Remade Division
New priorities. Dhillon shifted the division toward challenging DEI and race-conscious policies, religious discrimination, transgender athletes in women’s sports, Second Amendment rights and election integrity, Fox News reported. CBS News reported that she moved away from the division’s traditional focus on discrimination against historically marginalized groups. Under her, the department dismissed more than 50 decades-old school desegregation consent decrees, many in the Deep South. Supporters, including The Daily Signal, praised her use of the FACE Act against attacks on pregnancy resource centers, her prosecutions of people who disrupted worship services, and her suits against school policies that let staff withhold a student’s gender identity from parents.
Policing. She dropped pending consent decrees with the Minneapolis and Louisville police departments and rescinded misconduct findings against six other departments, CBS News reported. After immigration agents fatally shot two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during protests in Minneapolis earlier this year, the division did not initially open criminal civil rights investigations, breaking with long-standing practice. It later joined the Pretti case under public pressure.
Voting. The division sued 31 jurisdictions, mostly Democratic-led states and the District of Columbia, for unredacted voter rolls. Department lawyers later acknowledged in court that the data would be shared with the Department of Homeland Security for criminal and immigration enforcement. The department has lost 27 of those cases, CBS News reported. On Election Day, the division deployed more than 1,000 poll monitors, a record.
Staffing and style. More than 75% of the division’s staff left during her tenure, according to ABC News, which cited staffing figures provided to Congress. Dhillon told Fox she recruited more than 130 lawyers. She announced some investigations on social media, a break from past practice, and said in interviews that social media posts sometimes inspired them, CBS reported.
Reactions
Critics. Stacey Young, a former division attorney who founded the advocacy group Justice Connection, called Dhillon “the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history,” HuffPost reported. Young argued that ending police investigations and consent decrees left communities less safe, according to The Hill. Kristen Clarke, who led the division under President Biden and is now NAACP general counsel, said Dhillon had “destroyed the crown jewel of the Justice Department,” ABC News reported. Former division staff also published an open letter criticizing her leadership last December, The Hill noted.
Supporters. Blanche said Dhillon had defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor. Conservatives had argued from the start that the division had become ideologically tilted under previous administrations and needed redirecting, Fox News reported. Dhillon described the overhaul to Fox as finished work: the goal was to change the division, she said, and that was done.
What’s Next
Dhillon was born in 1969 in Chandigarh, India. Before joining the administration she founded Dhillon Law Group in San Francisco and the Center for American Liberty, a nonprofit litigating civil liberties cases, Axios reported. She built a national profile in First Amendment and election law cases. A longtime Republican Party official, she was vice chair of the California Republican Party and served as Republican National Committeewoman for California from 2016 until she joined the Justice Department.
Trump nominated her in December 2024, and she was sworn in in April 2025 after Senate confirmation. She told Fox News that she moved to Washington after the deaths of her husband and her father.
With Democrats taking control of Congress in January, Dhillon was asked whether she would testify if subpoenaed. She told Fox that executive privilege would limit what she could discuss and that she would follow legal counsel.
